Move the paper until you see a small band of colours. Newton did something similar with a glass prism and showed that white light is a mixture of all the colours.
myth: An apple fell on Newton's head and he suddenly discovered gravity.

Newton said seeing an apple fall in his garden made him wonder whether the same force reached up to the Moon. Nobody recorded it hitting his head. It took him about 20 more years of work to publish his law of gravity.
facts: Warden, then Master, of the Royal Mint

sec.t:
Newton was born in 1642 at Woolsthorpe Manor, a stone farmhouse in Lincolnshire. His father had died three months earlier. When Isaac was three, his mother remarried and left him with his grandmother. He grew up clever, quiet and often lonely.

At school he built model windmills, water clocks and sundials. His mother took him out of school to run the farm, but he was hopeless at it. A schoolmaster and an uncle persuaded her to send him to Trinity College, Cambridge, instead.

People had long seen colours appear when light passed through glass. Most thought the glass added the colours. Newton tested this. He let a beam of sunlight through a hole in his shutter, split it into colours with one [[prism|prism]], then used a second prism to join them back into white. Light, he showed, is a mix of colours. That is also why a [[@rainbow-how|rainbow]] always shows them in the same order.

Lenses in early telescopes made coloured blurs around stars, so Newton designed a telescope that used a curved mirror instead. His small reflecting telescope, built around 1668, was about 15 cm long. Today the biggest [[@telescopes-how|telescopes]] all use mirrors.

In 1687, encouraged by the [[astronomer|astronomer]] Edmond Halley, Newton published a book in Latin usually called the Principia. It set out his three laws of motion. An object keeps moving unless a force acts on it. A bigger force gives a bigger push. Every push has an equal push back, which is how [[@rockets-how|rockets]] fly.

It also showed that one law of gravity explains falling apples, the tides and the [[@spacecraft-move|orbits]] of planets. The book made him the most famous scientist in Europe. His work built on astronomers like [[@galileo|Galileo]], and he once wrote that he had seen further by "standing on the shoulders of giants".

In 1696 Newton moved to London to work at the Royal Mint. He tracked down counterfeiters and made sure coins had the right amount of silver. He was knighted in 1705.

He could be prickly. He argued bitterly with the German mathematician Leibniz over who invented calculus first. Historians now agree they developed it separately. Newton also spent years on alchemy, the old attempt to turn metals into gold, and on religious writings. He died in 1727 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.

text: A QR code is a square grid of black and white blocks. Each block is like one bit in [[@binary-code|binary]]: black can mean 1, white can mean 0. Together, the blocks spell out a message, often a web address or a payment address.

When you point your phone camera at a QR code, software finds the three big corner squares, works out the code's size and angle, and reads the pattern of blocks. It then turns those 1s and 0s back into letters and numbers. All of that takes a fraction of a second. Unlike a barcode, which holds information only from side to side, a QR code stores it both across and down. That is why it can carry so much more in a small square.

st.prompt: Why does a QR code have three big squares in its corners?

options.t: So the camera can find the code and tell which way up it is
They hold the most important part of the message
They are the company's logo

st.reveal: The three corner squares are called finder patterns. They let a camera spot the code instantly, from any angle, and work out which way it is turned. The missing fourth corner shows which way is up.

myth: Scanning a QR code is always safe.

A QR code is just a hidden link or message. Scammers sometimes stick fake codes over real ones, leading to fake websites or payment requests. Check where a code leads before you tap, and ask an adult if you aren't sure.

sec.t:
Codes get scratched, rained on and folded. So a QR code stores its message more than once, in a clever mathematical way called error correction. Extra blocks hold clues that let the reader rebuild missing parts.

At the highest setting, about 30 percent of the code can be damaged and it still works. That is why some companies print their logo right in the middle of a QR code. The reader simply treats the logo as damage and fills in the gap. The thin white border around the code matters too. It gives the camera a clean edge, so the code doesn't blur into the pattern behind it.

Codes also come in sizes. The smallest has 21 blocks on each side. The biggest has 177 on each side and can hold about 7,000 numbers.

Denso Wave owned a patent on the QR code, but it chose not to charge anyone for using the standard design. Anyone could print one, and any company could write software to read them.

That decision helped QR codes spread around the globe. For years they were common mainly in Japan and China. Then smartphone [[@cameras-how|cameras]] learned to read them without any special app, and during the COVID-19 [[pandemic|pandemic]], restaurants everywhere swapped paper menus for codes on the table.

sec.h: The square on the chai stall
sec.t:
In India, the QR code found its biggest job. With [[@upi-payments|UPI]], any shop can print a free QR code that carries its payment address. A tea seller, a flower vendor outside a temple and a taxi driver can all [[@digital-india|take digital payments]] with a sheet of laminated paper.

In the United States, QR codes are common on menus, tickets and boarding passes. In India they are on autorickshaw seat backs, temple donation boxes and the side of fruit carts. A tool built to track car parts now helps millions of people buy their morning tea.

text: Argentina is a large country covering much of the southern part of South America. It is about 3,700 kilometres long from north to south, so it holds almost every kind of [[climate|climate]]. The north has hot forests and giant waterfalls. The middle has flat grasslands called the pampas. The west is walled by the Andes, and the far south, Patagonia, is a land of wind, [[glacier|glaciers]] and [[@penguin-flight|penguins]].

Most Argentines live in cities, especially in and around the capital, Buenos Aires. Argentina is known for football, tango, beef cooked over open fires, and a drink called mate. [[@spanish-language|Spanish]] is the main language, spoken with an accent that many people say sounds a little Italian.

st.prompt: In Argentina, when does Christmas come?

options.t: In midsummer, often on a hot day
In the middle of winter, with snow
In the rainy season in spring

st.reveal: Argentina is in the Southern Hemisphere, so its seasons are the opposite of India's and the USA's. Christmas and New Year fall in summer, and many families celebrate with an evening barbecue outdoors. July is the coldest month.

sec.t:
Aconcagua, in the Andes on the border with Chile, is 6,961 metres high. No mountain outside Asia is taller. In the far south, the Perito Moreno Glacier pushes into a lake in a wall of ice about 70 metres high. Every so often, huge chunks break off and crash into the water with a noise like thunder. Unlike most [[@glaciers|glaciers]], it stayed roughly the same size for decades, though scientists reported in 2025 that it has started to shrink quickly.

In the north-east, on the border with Brazil, the Iguazú River tumbles over a curved cliff in about 275 separate waterfalls. The biggest is called the Devil's Throat. The spray is so thick that rainbows hang over the falls on sunny days.

sec.h: Gauchos, giants and the end of the world
sec.t:
On the pampas, cowboys called gauchos have herded cattle on horseback for centuries. The grasslands made Argentina one of the world's great beef producers, and the [[@bbq|asado]], a barbecue of meat cooked slowly over wood embers, is a weekend [[ritual|ritual]] for many families.

Patagonia hides another kind of giant. Some of the largest dinosaurs ever found were dug up there, including [[@argentinosaurus|Argentinosaurus]], a plant-eater that may have weighed as much as ten elephants.

At the very southern tip lies Ushuaia, often called the southernmost city in the world. Cruise ships and research ships leave from its harbour for Antarctica, about 1,000 kilometres away.

{{story:argentinosaurus}}

Between about 1880 and 1930, millions of people sailed to Argentina from Europe, especially Italy and Spain, looking for work and land. Today a large share of Argentines have Italian ancestors. That is why pizza and pasta are everyday food in Buenos Aires, and why Spanish there has a sing-song, Italian-sounding [[rhythm|rhythm]].

In the poor dockside neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires and Montevideo in the late 1800s, immigrants, locals and people of African descent mixed their music. Out of it came the tango, a dramatic dance for two, set to accordion-like bandoneon music. UNESCO listed it as world heritage in 2009.

In 1892, Argentine police used a bloody thumbprint left on a door frame to solve a murder. The detective, Eduardo Álvarez, had been trained by Juan Vucetich, a police official who had built a system for sorting prints. It is usually described as the first murder anywhere solved by [[@fingerprints|fingerprints]], and Vucetich's system was soon copied by police in many countries.

Football is close to a religion. Argentina has won the men's [[@pop-world-cup-trophy|World Cup]] three times, in 1978, 1986 and 2022. Diego Maradona led the team in 1986, and [[@messi-ronaldo|Lionel Messi]] lifted the trophy in 2022. Few rivalries are fiercer than [[@pele-maradona|Maradona]] versus Pelé of Brazil, argued over in cafés across both countries.

Argentina has an Indian connection too. In 1924, the poet [[@tagore|Rabindranath Tagore]] fell ill on a voyage and stayed for weeks near Buenos Aires as the guest of the writer Victoria Ocampo. They wrote to each other for the rest of his life.

text: In the [[monsoon|monsoon]], Cherrapunji is wrapped in cloud, roaring with waterfalls and drenched by rain that can fall for days on end. This small town in the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya, known locally as Sohra, is one of the wettest places on Earth.

It holds two world records from long ago. One is the most rain in a year, about 26,461 mm from August 1860 to July 1861. The other is the most in one calendar month, 9,300 mm in July 1861. In an ordinary year it still gets around 11,000 to 12,000 mm. Delhi gets about 800 mm a year. Mumbai, famous for its monsoon, gets about 2,200.
Nearby Mawsynram, about 15 km to the west, now usually gets slightly more rain on average, and is often called the wettest place on Earth.

st.reveal: In the monsoon, warm winds full of moisture blow north over the flat plains of Bangladesh and slam into the Khasi Hills. Pushed up the cliffs, the air cools quickly and its water vapour turns into rain.

sec.h: Why the rain piles up here
sec.t:
The answer is geography. From June to September, the monsoon winds blow north from the Bay of Bengal, heavy with water. They cross the flat, low plains of Bangladesh, with nothing to stop them.

Then they hit a wall. The Khasi Hills rise steeply, almost like cliffs, to more than 1,400 metres. The wet air is forced upward. As it rises, it cools, and cool air cannot hold as much water vapour. The vapour turns into droplets, the droplets join, and [[@clouds-rain|rain]] pours down on the hilltops.

Cherrapunji sits right at the edge of those cliffs, where the clouds first crash into the hills.

sec.h: Life under a hundred days of rain

sec.t:
The rain feeds some of India's most spectacular waterfalls. Nohkalikai Falls, near the town, drops about 340 metres in a single plunge, one of the highest in India. That is taller than the Eiffel Tower. Seven Sisters Falls spreads across a cliff in several streams during the monsoon.

The rain also explains the living root bridges. The Khasi people learned to guide the roots of rubber fig trees across streams, letting them grow into strong bridges over decades. Wooden bridges would rot in the endless wet, but [[@india-wonder-living-root-bridges|living root bridges]] grow stronger with age. Near the village of Nongriat, one is even a double-decker, with one bridge above another.

sec.h: The wettest town that runs dry
sec.t:
Here is the strangest part of Cherrapunji. After the monsoon, from about November to March, it barely rains at all. The hills around the town have lost much of their forest over the centuries, and the thin soil cannot hold the water. So the rain rushes off the cliffs and down into Bangladesh.

For years, families in Sohra have had to buy water from tankers or walk to springs in winter. Today, people collect rainwater on rooftops, plant trees and protect old forests to help the ground hold more.

So the town that once got 26 metres of rain in a year is also a lesson about water. How much the land can keep matters as much as how much falls. The places that stay greenest in Meghalaya are often the sacred forests, which Khasi communities have protected for generations, and where the soil can soak up the [[@monsoon|monsoon]] like a sponge.

text: Fantasy books take you to a world with rules different from ours. There might be magic, dragons, talking animals or a hidden school for wizards. That sense of stepping somewhere new is a big part of the fun.

But the best fantasy also feels real. Its worlds have maps, histories, languages and laws, so you can believe in them. And beneath the magic, the stories are about things everyone knows: being afraid, being brave, losing friends and finding them. Readers can think about hard problems from a safe distance. Fantasy also makes long series possible, and a world you love can keep you company for seven books.

myth: Fantasy is only for little children.
Some of the best-known fantasy was written by university professors, and adults buy a large share of fantasy books. Many fantasy stories deal with serious ideas like war, loss, power and friendship.

sec.t:
People have always told stories with magic in them. The [[@greek-myths|Greek myths]] have monsters and gods. The Ramayana and Mahabharata have flying chariots and enchanted weapons. The tales of [[@vikram-betal|Vikram and Betal]], where a ghost on a king's back asks riddles, are more than a thousand years old.

What changed in the 1900s was the idea of a whole invented world, written as a novel. Earlier writers like Lewis Carroll and L. Frank Baum, author of The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (1900), sent children into magic lands. But the modern shape of fantasy came mostly from two friends at Oxford.

In 1997, J. K. Rowling's first [[@harry-potter-effect|Harry Potter]] book came out with a small first print run. Within a few years, children around the world were queuing at midnight for new books. By 2023, the seven books had sold more than 600 million copies in more than 80 languages.

The books mixed magic with something ordinary: school. Children knew about lessons, homework, unfair teachers and best friends. That made the magic easy to step into.

Fantasy today comes from many cultures. Rick Riordan's Percy Jackson series puts Greek gods in modern America. Roshani Chokshi, an American writer with Indian roots, wrote the Aru Shah series, in which a 12-year-old girl finds herself mixed up with the gods and demons of Hindu stories.

In India, generations grew up on fantasy through comics and magazines such as Chandamama, full of kings, magic and clever [[trickster|tricksters]]. Many Indian writers now draw on Indian myths and folk tales for new fantasy novels.

Tolkien wrote that fantasy offers "escape", but he meant it in a good way, like a prisoner escaping a cell. Fantasy lets us picture a world where things could be different.

Some writers say fantasy helps young readers practise courage. A hobbit is small and scared, yet still carries the ring. A child reading that might feel a little braver at school the next day. Researchers who study reading and empathy have found mixed results, so nobody can say for sure that fantasy changes people. Readers, though, keep coming back. Fantasy has also spread to films and [[@video-games|video games]], where players can explore invented worlds for themselves.

text: Malayalam is the language of Kerala and [[@lakshadweep|Lakshadweep]], spoken as a first language by about 3.5 crore people in India and by many more in the Gulf countries and beyond. It is a Dravidian language, a close relative of Tamil.

A few things make it stand out. Its name is a palindrome. Its [[script|script]] has a large set of letters, with rounded shapes that look like loops and waves. It borrowed so many Sanskrit words that poets once wrote in a blend of the two. And Kerala, where it is spoken, has the highest literacy rate of any big Indian state, so Malayalam has an unusually large reading public.

st.reveal: Malayalam grew out of a western form of early Tamil spoken along the Kerala coast. Over the centuries, the Western Ghats mountains helped keep the two apart, and Malayalam took in many Sanskrit words. Speakers of the two can still catch some of each other's words.

myth: Malayalam is a dialect of Tamil.

Malayalam began as a western form of early Tamil, but it became a separate language more than a thousand years ago. It has its own script, grammar and literature, and its speakers cannot fully understand Tamil without learning it.

sec.t:
Around 2,000 years ago, people along the Kerala coast spoke an early form of [[@tamil-ancient|Tamil]]. The tall [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]] mountains separated them from Tamil speakers to the east, and over hundreds of years their speech drifted in its own direction.

The oldest known writing in Malayalam is the Vazhappally copper plate, from about 830 CE. It records a royal grant to a temple. By the 1200s, poems such as *Ramacharitam* were being written in a language clearly on its way to Malayalam.

Malayalam also traded words with the many visitors who came for Kerala's [[@cardamom-pepper|pepper]]. Arab, Jewish, Chinese and later Portuguese and Dutch traders landed at ports like [[@kochi|Kochi]]. The Malayalam word for a window, *janala*, comes from Portuguese.

{{story:kathakali}}

In [[medieval|medieval]] Kerala, poets loved to mix Malayalam with Sanskrit. They called this style Manipravalam, meaning "rubies and coral". The idea was that red rubies and red coral, strung together, make a beautiful necklace.

In the 1500s, the poet Thunchaththu Ezhuthachan retold the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] and Mahabharata in Malayalam. He is often called the father of modern Malayalam, and his version of the Ramayana is still read aloud in many Kerala homes during the [[monsoon|monsoon]] month of Karkidakam.

Malayalam stories also live on stage. [[@kathakali|Kathakali]], Kerala's famous dance-drama, uses songs in a style close to Manipravalam.

The Malayalam script comes from Grantha, a script once used to write Sanskrit in South India. It has more than 50 letters in its full set, and many consonants can join together into special combined shapes.

In 1872, a German missionary named Hermann Gundert published a Malayalam-English dictionary that is still respected. In the 1970s, the Kerala government simplified the script so it was easier to print on typewriters. Today you can see both older and newer letter forms on the same street. When computers arrived, volunteers in Kerala worked to bring back the older, more traditional letter shapes in free digital fonts, so that the script could look the way many readers preferred.

In 2013, Malayalam became the fifth language to be declared a classical language by the Government of India. Kerala's 2011 literacy rate was about 94%, the highest among India's states. Newspapers sell in huge numbers, and there are public libraries in villages across the state. Malayalam films are watched far beyond Kerala, often with subtitles. Malayalam writers have won the Jnanpith, India's highest literary award, several times, starting with the poet G. Sankara Kurup, who received the very first one in 1965.

Because so many Keralites work in the Gulf, Malayalam can be heard in shops and offices in Dubai, Doha and Muscat. Each year in late summer, from Kerala to the Gulf, families greet each other at [[@onam-pongal|Onam]] with the words *Onashamsakal*.
